claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel has an intact native oxide layer formed during manufacturing and storage.
The native oxide film on Q235 steel acts as a protective barrier against corrosion.
Removing the native oxide exposes the underlying steel substrate.
Removal of the native oxide accelerates electrochemical reactions on Q235 steel.
Removing the native oxide increases the rate and severity of Q235-steel corrosion in chloride-rich environments at room temperature.
Removing the native oxide increases the rate and severity of Q235-steel corrosion in chloride-rich environments at elevated temperature.
Native-oxide integrity mediates the diffusion of aggressive species to the steel surface.
Native-oxide integrity mediates the establishment of anodic sites on the steel surface.
A continuous native oxide limits direct contact between the Q235 substrate and chloride ions.
Limiting chloride contact retards localized electrochemical dissolution of Q235 steel.
Exposure of the underlying iron after oxide removal facilitates anodic oxidation.
Exposure of the underlying iron after oxide removal facilitates localized pitting and corrosion propagation.
Oxide-removed specimens will have greater weight loss than untreated controls under otherwise identical exposure conditions.
Oxide-removed specimens will exhibit more severe pitting than untreated controls under otherwise identical exposure conditions.
The magnitude of the corrosion-rate increase may depend on the completeness of oxide removal.
The magnitude of the corrosion-rate increase may depend on chloride concentration and temperature.
Microstructural variation within Q235 steel may affect the measured corrosion-rate increase.
